metadata.exam-title: Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate
metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Guide for the Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate exam - validates proficiency in building, deploying, and evaluating generative AI solutions on the Databricks platform.

question.title: LLM Application Architecture on Databricks
question.scenario: A data team is starting their first generative AI project on Databricks. They need to build a customer-facing chatbot that answers questions about product documentation. The team wants to use the simplest possible architecture.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature provides the most straightforward way to serve a foundation model for a chatbot application?

choices.choice: Foundation Model APIs with pay-per-token billing
Custom-trained model deployed to a GPU cluster
External model proxy through a third-party gateway
Fine-tuned model exported and hosted outside Databricks

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which option requires the least infrastructure setup and is purpose-built for quick adoption of foundation models.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Foundation Model APIs provide instant access to curated foundation models (like DBRX, Llama, Mixtral) through a simple REST API with pay-per-token pricing. There is no cluster provisioning, no model deployment pipeline, and no infrastructure management required. This is the fastest path to serving an LLM on Databricks for teams starting out.

ul.li: Foundation Model APIs are accessible via the /serving-endpoints REST API and are OpenAI-compatible, making migration from other providers straightforward.
Pay-per-token billing means you only pay for what you use, unlike provisioned throughput which requires capacity planning.
For production workloads with predictable traffic, provisioned throughput endpoints offer better cost efficiency and guaranteed latency.

question.title: Prompt Engineering for Structured Output
question.scenario: An engineer is building a pipeline that extracts product attributes from unstructured reviews. The downstream system requires a strict JSON schema with fields for sentiment, features_mentioned, and rating_estimate. The LLM occasionally returns malformed JSON.
question.question-text: Which prompt engineering technique is most effective at ensuring the LLM consistently returns valid, schema-compliant JSON?

choices.choice: Adding a system message that says "always return valid JSON"
Providing a concrete JSON example in the prompt with the exact schema and instructing the model to follow it precisely
Increasing the temperature parameter to explore more output formats
Using a longer context window to give the model more room for reasoning

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which technique gives the model the clearest structural template to follow, reducing ambiguity in the expected output format.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Few-shot prompting with a concrete JSON example (including the exact field names and value types) is the most reliable way to get consistent structured output. The model can pattern-match against the example, reducing schema drift. A vague instruction like "return valid JSON" gives no structural guidance. Increasing temperature increases randomness, making format compliance worse. Context window length does not affect output formatting.

ul.li: For maximum reliability, combine few-shot examples with response_format={"type": "json_object"} when the serving endpoint supports it.
Chain-of-thought prompting can improve extraction accuracy but should place reasoning before the JSON block to avoid corrupting the structured output.
Guardrails or Pydantic-based output parsers can validate and retry on malformed responses as a defense-in-depth layer.

question.title: Compound AI System Design
question.scenario: A financial services company wants to build a system that can answer complex regulatory compliance questions. The system must cite specific regulation sections, cross-reference multiple documents, and explain reasoning step by step. A single LLM call is insufficient for the task.
question.question-text: Which architectural pattern best addresses the need for multi-step reasoning with source attribution?

choices.choice: A single large-context model with all regulations concatenated into the prompt
A fine-tuned model trained on regulation question-answer pairs
A compound AI system combining retrieval, chain-of-thought prompting, and citation generation in a multi-step pipeline
A batch inference job that pre-generates answers for all possible questions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which approach decomposes the problem into specialized steps rather than relying on a single model call to do everything.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A compound AI system orchestrates multiple components: a retriever finds relevant regulation sections, a chain-of-thought prompt guides the LLM through step-by-step reasoning, and a citation generator maps claims back to source documents. This modular approach outperforms a single monolithic call because each stage can be independently optimized and debugged. Stuffing all regulations into context exceeds token limits and degrades accuracy. Fine-tuning alone cannot guarantee citation accuracy. Pre-generating answers is infeasible for open-ended questions.

ul.li: Compound AI systems are a core Databricks pattern — Mosaic AI Agent Framework is built around this concept of orchestrating retrieval, generation, and tool use.
Each component in the pipeline can be evaluated independently: retrieval precision, reasoning correctness, and citation faithfulness are separate metrics.
This architecture also enables hybrid approaches where different LLMs handle different stages based on cost-performance trade-offs.

question.title: Governance with Unity Catalog for GenAI
question.scenario: An enterprise is deploying multiple GenAI applications across departments. Each department has its own data, models, and serving endpoints. The security team requires centralized access control, lineage tracking, and auditability across all GenAI assets.
question.question-text: Which Databricks capability provides unified governance over models, vector indexes, serving endpoints, and training data for GenAI workloads?

choices.choice: Workspace-level access control lists applied to each notebook
Separate IAM policies configured in the cloud provider console
A custom metadata catalog built on Delta tables
Unity Catalog with its centralized permission model and lineage tracking

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which Databricks service provides a single governance layer across all data and AI assets, not just tables.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Unity Catalog extends governance to all GenAI assets: registered models, vector search indexes, model serving endpoints, feature tables, and training datasets. It provides a centralized permission model (GRANT/REVOKE) across workspaces, automatic lineage tracking from data to model to endpoint, and full audit logging. Workspace-level ACLs are too granular and don't span workspaces. Cloud IAM is external and doesn't understand Databricks-specific asset types. A custom metadata catalog would require building governance from scratch.

ul.li: Unity Catalog tracks lineage from source tables through feature engineering, model training, and deployment — critical for compliance and debugging.
Model aliases in Unity Catalog (Champion/Challenger) enable safe model promotion workflows without changing serving endpoint configurations.
Row-level and column-level security in Unity Catalog can restrict what training data different teams can access, supporting data minimization principles.

question.title: Selecting a GenAI Use Case
question.scenario: A retail company is evaluating several potential GenAI projects. The team has limited ML experience and wants to start with a use case that delivers quick value with minimal risk. They are considering customer support automation, autonomous inventory management, product description generation, and real-time fraud detection with LLMs.
question.question-text: Which use case is the best starting point for a team new to generative AI?

choices.choice: Product description generation from structured catalog data, which has low risk and easily verifiable output
Autonomous inventory management decisions without human review
Real-time fraud detection powered entirely by an LLM
Fully automated customer support replacing all human agents

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which use case has the lowest consequences for errors and produces output that humans can easily review before publishing.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Product description generation is ideal for a first GenAI project: the input (structured catalog data) is clean, the output (marketing text) is easily reviewed by humans, errors are low-stakes (a bad description can be edited), and success is straightforward to measure. Autonomous inventory management and fraud detection carry high financial risk if the model errs. Fully replacing human support agents requires sophisticated guardrails and escalation paths that a new team is unlikely to build correctly.

ul.li: Databricks recommends a crawl-walk-run approach: start with human-in-the-loop use cases, then gradually increase automation as confidence and tooling mature.
Content generation use cases also produce natural training data for evaluation — each human edit becomes a preference signal for future improvement.
High-risk use cases like fraud detection are better served by traditional ML models that produce calibrated probabilities rather than by generative models.

question.title: System Prompt Design for Safety
question.scenario: A healthcare company is deploying a patient-facing chatbot that answers questions about medication side effects. The chatbot must never provide dosage recommendations, must always include a disclaimer to consult a physician, and must refuse to answer questions outside its scope.
question.question-text: Which approach best enforces these behavioral constraints in the chatbot?

choices.choice: Training users to only ask appropriate questions
A structured system prompt with explicit behavioral rules, refusal instructions, and mandatory disclaimer templates
Post-processing all responses with regex to remove dosage numbers
Limiting the context window so the model cannot generate long responses

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about where behavioral rules should be defined so they apply to every interaction, regardless of what the user asks.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A well-structured system prompt is the primary mechanism for constraining LLM behavior. By explicitly listing prohibited actions (no dosage advice), required elements (always include disclaimer), and scope boundaries (refuse off-topic questions), the model receives clear instructions on every request. User training is unreliable. Regex post-processing is brittle and misses paraphrased dosages. Context window limits affect length, not content quality.

ul.li: Defense-in-depth is best practice: combine system prompts with output guardrails (Mosaic AI Guardrails) and input classifiers to catch prompt injection attacks.
System prompts should be tested adversarially — red-teaming with jailbreak attempts helps identify gaps before deployment.
Databricks AI Playground allows rapid iteration on system prompts with side-by-side model comparison before committing to a production configuration.

question.title: Multi-tenant GenAI Architecture
question.scenario: A SaaS company needs to serve different LLM configurations to different customers from a shared Databricks workspace. Each tenant has unique system prompts, retrieval sources, and usage quotas. The architecture must prevent data leakage between tenants while keeping infrastructure costs shared.
question.question-text: Which design pattern ensures tenant isolation in a shared GenAI serving infrastructure?

choices.choice: A single prompt template with the tenant name injected as a variable
Separate Databricks workspaces for every tenant
Tenant-scoped configurations routed through a shared serving endpoint, with Unity Catalog enforcing data-level access control per tenant
A dedicated GPU cluster per tenant running independent model copies

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which approach balances cost efficiency from shared infrastructure with data isolation enforced at the governance layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Routing tenant-specific configurations (system prompts, retrieval indexes, quotas) through a shared serving endpoint keeps infrastructure costs low. Unity Catalog enforces data-level isolation so tenant A's retrieval sources are never accessible to tenant B's queries. Simply injecting tenant names provides no real isolation. Separate workspaces or dedicated GPU clusters per tenant are cost-prohibitive and operationally complex for a SaaS product.

ul.li: The routing layer should resolve tenant context from the authentication token and inject the correct system prompt and vector search index before the LLM call.
Unity Catalog's row-level security can partition a shared vector index by tenant_id, enabling physical resource sharing with logical data isolation.
Rate limiting and token quotas per tenant can be implemented at the API gateway layer using Databricks Model Serving's built-in rate limiting or an external gateway.

question.title: Temperature Parameter in LLM Inference
question.scenario: An engineer is configuring an LLM endpoint for two different tasks: a creative marketing copy generator and a factual Q&A system for internal documentation. Both use the same underlying model but need different output characteristics.
question.question-text: How should the temperature parameter differ between these two use cases?

choices.choice: Both should use a temperature of 1.0 for consistency
The marketing copy generator should use a lower temperature than the Q&A system
Temperature has no effect on output variability
The marketing copy generator should use a higher temperature for creativity, while the Q&A system should use a lower temperature for factual precision

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about how temperature controls randomness — one task benefits from variety while the other needs determinism.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Temperature controls the randomness of token selection during generation. A higher temperature (e.g., 0.7-1.0) increases diversity and creativity, which benefits marketing copy that should be varied and engaging. A lower temperature (e.g., 0.0-0.3) makes output more deterministic and focused, which is essential for factual Q&A where consistency and accuracy matter more than novelty. Using the same temperature for both ignores their fundamentally different requirements.

ul.li: Temperature of 0 makes the model greedy (always picks the highest-probability token), which maximizes consistency but can lead to repetitive output.
top_p (nucleus sampling) is often used alongside temperature — for factual tasks, low temperature with top_p=0.9 balances accuracy with natural phrasing.
Databricks Model Serving endpoints allow per-request temperature overrides, so a single endpoint can serve both use cases with different parameters.

question.title: RAG Overview and Purpose
question.scenario: A legal firm wants their LLM to answer questions using the firm's proprietary case law database, which is updated weekly. The LLM's training data does not include this proprietary information and cannot be retrained weekly.
question.question-text: Which technique allows the LLM to use the firm's proprietary data without retraining the model?

choices.choice: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, which fetches relevant documents at query time and includes them in the LLM's context
Increasing the model's parameter count to store more knowledge
Using a higher temperature to encourage the model to generate novel legal interpretations
Caching all previous LLM responses for reuse

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which approach dynamically injects external knowledge into the model's context at inference time rather than baking it into model weights.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge base at query time and includes them in the LLM's prompt context. This allows the model to answer based on up-to-date proprietary data without retraining. The knowledge base can be refreshed independently of the model. Increasing parameter count doesn't add specific proprietary knowledge. Higher temperature increases randomness, not knowledge. Response caching doesn't help with novel questions.

ul.li: RAG decouples knowledge from model parameters — the model provides reasoning capability while the retrieval system provides factual grounding.
On Databricks, RAG pipelines typically use Databricks Vector Search for retrieval, which integrates with Delta tables for automatic index synchronization.
RAG is preferred over fine-tuning when the knowledge base changes frequently because updating an index is much cheaper and faster than retraining a model.

question.title: Databricks Vector Search Configuration
question.scenario: A team is setting up Databricks Vector Search for their RAG application. Their source documents are stored in a Delta table that receives daily updates. They need the vector index to stay synchronized with the Delta table without manual reindexing.
question.question-text: Which Databricks Vector Search index type automatically stays synchronized with its source Delta table?

choices.choice: A direct vector access index where embeddings are pre-computed externally
A Delta Sync Index, which automatically syncs with the source Delta table as data changes
A batch-refreshed index that requires a manual trigger after each update
A streaming index built on Structured Streaming that requires a separate cluster

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the index type that has built-in synchronization with Delta table change feeds, requiring no manual intervention.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A Delta Sync Index in Databricks Vector Search automatically stays current with its source Delta table using Delta's Change Data Feed (CDF). When rows are inserted, updated, or deleted in the source table, the index reflects those changes without manual reindexing. A direct vector access index requires you to manage embeddings and updates yourself. There is no separate "batch-refreshed" or "streaming" index type — Delta Sync handles synchronization natively.

ul.li: Delta Sync Indexes can be configured as either "triggered" (sync on demand) or "continuous" (near real-time sync with sub-second latency).
The index can compute embeddings automatically using a specified embedding model endpoint, or you can provide a pre-computed embedding column.
Unity Catalog governs access to vector search indexes — query permissions are inherited from the source table's ACLs.

question.title: Chunking Strategy for Technical Documentation
question.scenario: A software company is building a RAG system over their API documentation. The documents contain code examples interspersed with explanatory text. When chunks split a code block from its explanation, the retrieved context is incomplete and the LLM generates incorrect code.
question.question-text: Which chunking strategy best preserves the relationship between code blocks and their explanations?

choices.choice: Fixed-size chunking with 512-token windows
Character-level splitting at every newline
Semantic or structure-aware chunking that keeps code blocks and their surrounding explanatory text together as a unit
Sentence-level chunking that splits at every period

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which strategy uses the document's own structure to determine chunk boundaries rather than arbitrary token or character counts.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Semantic or structure-aware chunking respects document structure by using headings, code fences, and paragraph boundaries to define chunks. This keeps a code block and its explanatory text in the same chunk, preserving the context the LLM needs to generate accurate responses. Fixed-size chunking blindly cuts at token boundaries, often splitting code mid-function. Character or sentence splitting is even more granular and will fragment code blocks further.

ul.li: Recursive character text splitting (from LangChain) can approximate structure-aware chunking by splitting on markdown headers first, then paragraphs, then sentences.
Overlap between chunks (e.g., 10-20% of chunk size) helps preserve context at boundaries but does not substitute for structure-aware splitting.
For API docs specifically, splitting by endpoint or section header and including the full endpoint signature in each chunk provides the best retrieval relevance.

question.title: Embedding Model Selection
question.scenario: A multinational company needs their RAG system to support queries in English, Spanish, French, and German. Their current embedding model was trained only on English text, causing poor retrieval for non-English queries even when relevant documents exist in those languages.
question.question-text: What is the most effective way to improve cross-lingual retrieval quality?

choices.choice: Translating all queries to English before embedding them
Using separate vector indexes for each language
Increasing the number of retrieved chunks to compensate for lower relevance
Switching to a multilingual embedding model that maps semantically similar text across languages into nearby vector space regions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which approach handles multilingual semantics natively in the embedding space rather than working around the limitation.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A multilingual embedding model (such as multilingual-e5 or BGE-M3) is trained to produce vectors where semantically equivalent text in different languages maps to similar regions. A Spanish query about "machine learning" will be near an English document about the same topic. Translation adds latency and loses nuance. Separate indexes per language prevent cross-lingual discovery. Retrieving more chunks wastes context on irrelevant results.

ul.li: Databricks Model Serving can host open-source multilingual embedding models like BGE-M3 or multilingual-e5-large on GPU endpoints.
When evaluating multilingual embeddings, test retrieval recall separately for each language pair — performance often varies significantly between high-resource and low-resource language pairs.
Hybrid search (combining vector similarity with BM25 keyword matching) can improve multilingual retrieval by catching cognates and technical terms that embed poorly but match lexically.

question.title: Vector Search Similarity Metrics
question.scenario: An engineer is configuring Databricks Vector Search for a document retrieval system. They need to choose a similarity metric. The documents are embedded using a model that produces normalized vectors (unit length). The engineer wants the most common and effective metric for this scenario.
question.question-text: Which similarity metric is most appropriate for normalized embedding vectors in Databricks Vector Search?

choices.choice: Cosine similarity, which measures the angle between vectors and is equivalent to dot product for normalized vectors
Euclidean distance, which measures straight-line distance in embedding space
Jaccard similarity, which compares set overlap between token lists
Manhattan distance, which sums absolute coordinate differences

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For normalized vectors (unit length), think about which metric focuses on directional similarity rather than magnitude.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, making it purely directional. When vectors are normalized to unit length, cosine similarity and dot product produce identical rankings. This is the standard metric for text embedding retrieval because most modern embedding models produce normalized vectors. Euclidean distance is valid but less common for text embeddings. Jaccard similarity operates on sets, not dense vectors. Manhattan distance is rarely used for embedding similarity.

ul.li: Databricks Vector Search supports cosine similarity, dot product, and L2 (Euclidean) distance as configurable metrics at index creation time.
For normalized vectors, cosine similarity and dot product give the same ranking order, but dot product is computationally cheaper since it skips the normalization step.
The choice of metric should match the embedding model's training objective — models trained with contrastive loss on cosine similarity should be queried with cosine similarity.

question.title: Hybrid Search for RAG
question.scenario: A customer support RAG system retrieves help articles using vector search. However, users frequently search for specific error codes (like ERR-4012) and product SKUs that embed poorly because they are arbitrary identifiers, not semantic concepts. Relevant articles exist but are not retrieved.
question.question-text: What retrieval improvement would best address poor recall for keyword-specific queries like error codes?

choices.choice: Increasing the embedding model's dimension size
Adding hybrid search that combines vector similarity with BM25 keyword matching to catch exact identifier matches
Re-embedding the entire corpus with a larger chunk size
Adding more few-shot examples to the retrieval query

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which technique supplements semantic search with exact keyword matching for terms that don't carry semantic meaning.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Hybrid search combines vector (semantic) retrieval with BM25 (keyword) retrieval and merges the results. Error codes and SKUs are arbitrary strings that don't carry semantic meaning, so they embed poorly. BM25 excels at exact and partial keyword matches, catching these identifiers reliably. Increasing embedding dimensions doesn't help with non-semantic tokens. Larger chunks don't improve identifier embedding quality. Few-shot examples apply to generation, not retrieval.

ul.li: Databricks Vector Search supports hybrid search by combining vector similarity scores with keyword match scores using reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).
Metadata filters in Vector Search can further narrow results by product category or document type before similarity ranking, improving precision for structured queries.
An alternative approach is to store error codes as metadata fields and use filtered search (vector search + metadata filter) rather than relying on embedding them.

question.title: RAG Context Window Management
question.scenario: A RAG pipeline retrieves 20 document chunks for each query to maximize recall. However, the LLM's responses have degraded — it frequently ignores relevant chunks positioned in the middle of the context and sometimes contradicts information from the retrieved documents.
question.question-text: What is the most likely cause of the LLM ignoring relevant retrieved content?

choices.choice: The embedding model is producing low-quality vectors
The LLM's tokenizer is truncating the input
The "lost in the middle" effect, where LLMs attend less to information positioned in the middle of long contexts
The vector search index is returning duplicate chunks

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the well-documented attention pattern where LLMs focus on the beginning and end of their context window, underweighting middle content.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The "lost in the middle" phenomenon is a well-studied LLM behavior where models attend strongly to the beginning and end of the context window but underweight information in the middle. With 20 retrieved chunks, the most relevant chunk might land in position 8-15, where it receives less attention. Mitigation strategies include retrieving fewer but higher-quality chunks, reranking to place the most relevant content at the beginning, or summarizing retrieved content before injection.

ul.li: A reranker (like a cross-encoder) can score each chunk against the query and reorder them by relevance before context injection, placing the best chunks at the beginning.
Reducing the number of retrieved chunks from 20 to 5-10 high-quality ones often improves answer quality because it reduces noise and keeps content in the attended window region.
Map-reduce strategies process each chunk independently (map) and then synthesize the results (reduce), eliminating the lost-in-the-middle problem at the cost of additional LLM calls.

question.title: Query Transformation for RAG
question.scenario: Users of a RAG-powered research assistant frequently ask vague questions like "tell me about the new feature" without specifying which product or feature. The retriever returns irrelevant results because the query lacks sufficient specificity for effective embedding similarity matching.
question.question-text: Which technique improves retrieval quality for vague or underspecified user queries?

choices.choice: Increasing the number of returned results from 5 to 50
Disabling the retrieval step and relying on the LLM's parametric knowledge
Reducing chunk sizes to capture more granular information
Query expansion or rewriting, where the LLM reformulates the vague query into a more specific search query before retrieval

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about adding a preprocessing step that transforms the user's query into a better search query before it reaches the retriever.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Query expansion (or rewriting) uses the LLM to reformulate a vague user query into a more specific search query before retrieval. For example, "tell me about the new feature" might become "describe the latest release features for Product X based on Q4 2025 changelog." This produces a more specific embedding that retrieves relevant documents. Returning more results amplifies noise. Disabling retrieval defeats the purpose of RAG. Smaller chunks increase fragmentation without addressing query quality.

ul.li: HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embedding) is an advanced query transformation that generates a hypothetical answer and uses its embedding for retrieval, often outperforming direct query embedding.
Multi-query retrieval generates multiple reformulations of the original query, retrieves for each, and merges results — increasing recall at the cost of additional LLM and retrieval calls.
Conversation history can provide context for query expansion — the LLM can resolve "the new feature" by referencing the product discussed in prior turns.

question.title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning Decision
question.scenario: A company needs their LLM to use a knowledge base of 10,000 internal policy documents that change monthly. They are debating whether to fine-tune a model on these documents or implement a RAG pipeline. Budget and turnaround time are constrained.
question.question-text: Why is RAG a better fit than fine-tuning for this use case?

choices.choice: RAG avoids costly retraining by updating the knowledge base independently of the model, and changes are reflected immediately
Fine-tuning is always superior to RAG for domain-specific knowledge
RAG does not require any LLM at all
RAG requires a larger upfront compute investment but is more accurate long-term

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which approach decouples the knowledge from the model so that monthly document changes don't require retraining.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: RAG separates knowledge (stored in a vector index) from reasoning (the LLM). When documents change monthly, only the vector index needs updating — a fast, inexpensive operation compared to fine-tuning. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights, requiring full retraining cycles every time documents change. RAG also provides source attribution, letting users verify answers against the original documents. Fine-tuning is not always superior — it excels at style and format adaptation but is expensive for frequently changing factual knowledge.

ul.li: RAG and fine-tuning are complementary, not mutually exclusive — you can fine-tune a model to better follow RAG-specific instructions while using retrieval for factual grounding.
Databricks Delta Sync Indexes update automatically when source Delta tables change, making the RAG knowledge update fully automated.
Fine-tuning is better suited for teaching the model a new output format, domain-specific terminology, or stylistic preferences that don't change frequently.

question.title: Model Serving Endpoint Types
question.scenario: A team needs to deploy an LLM for a production application that handles 500 concurrent users with strict latency requirements of under 200ms per token. The traffic is predictable during business hours but drops to near zero overnight.
question.question-text: Which Databricks Model Serving configuration best balances cost and performance for this traffic pattern?

choices.choice: Pay-per-token Foundation Model APIs with no dedicated compute
Provisioned throughput endpoint with scale-to-zero configured during off-peak hours
A static always-on cluster sized for peak traffic
Batch inference jobs scheduled hourly to pre-generate responses

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the option that guarantees dedicated compute during peak hours but avoids paying for idle capacity overnight.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Provisioned throughput endpoints provide dedicated GPU compute with guaranteed latency SLAs, meeting the 200ms/token requirement during business hours. Configuring scale-to-zero allows the endpoint to shut down overnight when traffic drops, eliminating idle compute costs. Pay-per-token APIs don't guarantee latency at high concurrency. A static cluster wastes money overnight. Batch inference can't serve real-time interactive users.

ul.li: Provisioned throughput is measured in tokens per second and auto-scales horizontally within configured min/max concurrency limits.
Scale-to-zero has a cold-start penalty (typically 2-5 minutes for GPU endpoints), so applications should implement a warm-up mechanism or accept initial latency spikes.
For hybrid traffic patterns, a small always-on baseline with autoscaling for bursts balances responsiveness with cost better than pure scale-to-zero.

question.title: Foundation Model APIs on Databricks
question.scenario: A data scientist wants to quickly prototype a text summarization feature. They do not want to manage model downloads, GPU clusters, or deployment pipelines. They want an API they can call immediately from a notebook.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature lets the data scientist call a foundation model instantly without any deployment setup?

choices.choice: Custom model training on a Spark cluster
Downloading a model from Hugging Face and deploying it manually
Foundation Model APIs, which provide instant access to pre-deployed models through a REST API
Creating a Docker container with the model and registering it as a service

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the zero-setup option that provides immediate API access to curated models without infrastructure management.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Foundation Model APIs on Databricks provide instant access to curated foundation models (DBRX, Llama, Mixtral, and others) through a simple REST API or Python SDK. No model download, GPU provisioning, or deployment pipeline is needed — the models are pre-deployed and ready to call from any notebook. This is the fastest path from idea to working prototype. Custom training, manual HuggingFace deployment, and Docker containerization all require significant setup.

ul.li: Foundation Model APIs are OpenAI-compatible, so existing code using the OpenAI SDK can be pointed at Databricks endpoints with minimal changes.
Available model classes include chat completion, embedding, and text completion — covering the most common GenAI tasks.
For prototyping, AI Playground in the Databricks UI provides a no-code interface to test models and system prompts before writing any code.

question.title: External Model Integration
question.scenario: A company uses GPT-4 from OpenAI for their production chatbot but wants to route all LLM calls through Databricks for centralized logging, access control, and cost tracking. They do not want to change their application code significantly.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature enables routing external LLM calls through Databricks for governance without changing the underlying model provider?

choices.choice: Fine-tuning a Databricks-hosted model to match GPT-4 behavior
Rewriting the application to use Databricks SQL instead of LLM calls
Deploying a local copy of GPT-4 on Databricks infrastructure
External Models in Model Serving, which proxies calls to external providers like OpenAI through a Databricks endpoint

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the feature that acts as a managed proxy, forwarding requests to external providers while adding Databricks governance.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: External Models in Databricks Model Serving create a Databricks endpoint that proxies requests to external providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, etc.). The application calls the Databricks endpoint using the same OpenAI-compatible API, and Databricks forwards the request to the external provider. This enables centralized access control via Unity Catalog, request/response logging for audit, rate limiting, and cost tracking — all without changing the underlying model or significantly modifying application code.

ul.li: External model endpoints support AI Gateway features: rate limiting, usage tracking, guardrails, and request/response logging to an inference table.
API keys for external providers are stored securely in Databricks Secrets, not in application code or environment variables.
Because external models use the same serving endpoint interface, you can A/B test a Databricks-hosted model against an external model by routing traffic between two endpoints.

question.title: Model Selection Trade-offs

The proprietary API model for maximum quality regardless of cost
The 70B model for maximum quality with data privacy
Using no LLM and relying entirely on rule-based keyword matching

question.title: Optimizing LLM Inference Throughput
question.scenario: A production serving endpoint for a 13B parameter LLM is hitting throughput limits during peak hours. The P99 latency exceeds the SLA. The team has a fixed GPU budget and cannot add more hardware. They need to serve more requests per second on the same infrastructure.
question.question-text: Which inference optimization technique would most effectively increase throughput within the existing GPU budget?

choices.choice: Switching from greedy decoding to beam search for higher quality
Increasing the maximum sequence length to give the model more room
Disabling logging and monitoring to free up compute resources
Applying model quantization (e.g., INT8 or INT4) to reduce memory footprint and increase batch size per GPU

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which technique reduces the model's memory footprint per GPU, enabling more concurrent requests on the same hardware.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Model quantization (INT8 or INT4) reduces the precision of model weights from 16-bit floats to 8-bit or 4-bit integers. This dramatically reduces GPU memory usage, allowing larger batch sizes and higher throughput on the same hardware. Modern quantization techniques (like GPTQ, AWQ, or bitsandbytes) maintain acceptable quality for most applications. Beam search increases compute per request, reducing throughput. Increasing sequence length uses more memory. Disabling monitoring is negligible and loses observability.

ul.li: Continuous batching (also called iteration-level batching) dynamically fills GPU capacity as requests finish, significantly improving throughput compared to static batching.
PagedAttention (used in vLLM) optimizes KV-cache memory allocation, reducing memory waste and enabling higher concurrency for long-context requests.
Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to predict multiple tokens that the larger model then verifies in parallel, improving throughput by 2-3x for some workloads.

question.title: Function Calling with LLMs

question.question-text: Which capability enables the LLM to invoke backend APIs with structured parameters?

choices.choice: Increasing the model's context window to include API documentation
Function calling (tool use), where the LLM generates structured function calls that the application executes against backend APIs
Training the LLM to output curl commands as plain text
Pre-generating all possible API responses and storing them in the context

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the mechanism where the LLM decides which function to call and with what arguments, while the application handles actual execution.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Function calling (also called tool use) allows the LLM to generate structured function call requests (function name + JSON arguments) based on user intent. The application intercepts these requests, executes the corresponding backend API calls, and returns the results to the LLM for incorporation into its response. This keeps the LLM in a reasoning/planning role while the application handles execution. Including API docs in context doesn't enable execution. Outputting curl commands is fragile and unsafe. Pre-generating responses is infeasible for real-time data.

ul.li: Databricks Model Serving endpoints support function calling through the OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions API with a tools parameter.
Tool definitions include the function name, description, and parameter JSON schema — the LLM uses these to select the right tool and format arguments correctly.
Parallel function calling allows the LLM to request multiple tool calls in a single response, reducing round trips for queries that need data from multiple sources.

question.title: Agent Architecture with Planning
question.scenario: A research assistant agent must handle complex multi-step tasks like "find recent papers on quantum computing published by MIT, summarize their methods sections, and compare them in a table." This requires decomposing the task into subtasks, executing them in sequence with dependencies, and synthesizing results.
question.question-text: Which agent architecture pattern is most suitable for complex multi-step tasks with dependencies between steps?

choices.choice: A simple prompt that asks the LLM to do everything in a single response
A round-robin tool caller that invokes each tool once in a fixed order
Running all tools in parallel and concatenating their outputs
A ReAct-style agent with a planning step that decomposes the task into a dependency graph and executes subtasks iteratively with reasoning at each step

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the pattern that combines reasoning about what to do next with action execution in an iterative loop, handling dependencies between steps.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) agent interleaves reasoning (what should I do next and why?) with action (execute a tool call) in a loop. For complex tasks, a planning step first decomposes the request into subtasks with dependencies (search papers -> for each paper, extract methods -> compile comparison table). The agent then executes each subtask, using the output of previous steps as input to subsequent ones. A single prompt can't reliably handle multi-step tasks. Fixed-order or parallel execution can't handle dependencies between steps.

ul.li: Mosaic AI Agent Framework supports ReAct-style agents with configurable tool sets, conversation memory, and built-in tracing for debugging agent decision paths.
Plan-and-execute patterns (generate full plan, then execute) are faster but more brittle than ReAct (plan one step, execute, observe, plan next) for tasks where early results change the plan.
Agent evaluations should test both the final output quality and the trace quality (did the agent take reasonable steps?), since agents can arrive at correct answers through unreliable paths.

question.title: AI Agent Concept
question.scenario: A product team is learning about AI agents. They understand that LLMs can generate text, but they are unclear on what makes an "agent" different from a simple chatbot. They want a clear explanation of the core capability that distinguishes an agent.
question.question-text: What core capability distinguishes an AI agent from a simple LLM chatbot?

choices.choice: An agent can autonomously decide which tools to call and take actions in external systems based on the conversation, while a chatbot only generates text responses
An agent uses a larger model than a chatbot
An agent can only respond with pre-written templates
An agent does not use an LLM at all

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the key difference: one generates text only, while the other can reason about and invoke actions in the real world.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An AI agent extends an LLM with the ability to take actions: it can decide which tools to call (database queries, API calls, file operations), execute those actions, observe the results, and continue reasoning. A simple chatbot generates text responses without interacting with external systems. The distinction is about agency — the ability to act on the world, not just describe it. Agents typically use the same LLMs as chatbots; the difference is the tool-use orchestration layer, not model size.

ul.li: The agent loop (reason -> select tool -> execute -> observe -> reason again) is the fundamental pattern, whether implemented as ReAct, function-calling chains, or custom orchestration.
Databricks Mosaic AI Agent Framework provides the scaffolding for building agents with tool definitions, memory, guardrails, and evaluation — avoiding the need to build the loop from scratch.
Agent safety requires careful tool permission design — an agent should only have access to the minimum set of tools needed for its purpose, following the principle of least privilege.

question.title: Agent Guardrails and Safety
question.scenario: An AI agent has access to tools that can read customer data, execute SQL queries, and send emails. During testing, the agent was tricked by a prompt injection in a customer record to send an email with sensitive data to an external address. The team needs to prevent this class of attack.
question.question-text: Which combination of safeguards most effectively prevents prompt injection attacks from causing the agent to take harmful actions?

choices.choice: Blocking all special characters in user input
Input guardrails that detect injection patterns, tool-level permissions that restrict email recipients to approved domains, and output guardrails that flag sensitive data in outbound actions
Training users to avoid including suspicious text in customer records
Reducing the agent's context window to limit how much injected text it can process

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider a defense-in-depth approach that applies checks at multiple layers: input validation, tool-level restrictions, and output inspection.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Defense-in-depth is essential for agent safety: input guardrails use classifiers to detect prompt injection attempts in both user messages and retrieved content; tool-level permissions restrict what actions the agent can take (e.g., emails only to approved domains); output guardrails inspect outbound actions for sensitive data patterns (PII, credentials) before execution. No single layer is sufficient — injection detection has false negatives, so tool-level and output restrictions act as backstops. Blocking special characters breaks legitimate input. User training is unreliable. Context window limits don't prevent injection.

ul.li: Mosaic AI Guardrails provides configurable input/output filters for toxicity, PII, prompt injection, and custom safety rules that can be attached to any serving endpoint.
Human-in-the-loop approval for high-risk actions (sending emails, modifying data, executing payments) is a critical safety layer for production agents.
Indirect prompt injection (injection via retrieved documents or tool outputs, not direct user input) is especially dangerous because it bypasses input-only defenses.

question.title: Tool Definition Best Practices
question.scenario: A developer is defining tools for an AI agent. The agent has access to a tool called "query_database" but keeps calling it with incorrect parameters, causing errors. The tool definition has a vague description and no parameter schema.
question.question-text: What is the most important improvement to help the agent call tools correctly?

choices.choice: Increasing the agent's temperature to explore more parameter combinations
Removing the tool and having the agent generate SQL directly
Providing clear, detailed tool descriptions with precise parameter names, types, constraints, and examples in the JSON schema
Adding more tools so the agent has alternatives if one fails

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The LLM selects tools and fills parameters based on their descriptions and schemas — better descriptions lead to better tool use.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Clear tool descriptions and precise parameter JSON schemas are the primary way the LLM understands how to use a tool. The description should explain what the tool does and when to use it. Each parameter should have a name, type, description, required/optional status, and constraints (enums, ranges, formats). Examples in the description further reduce ambiguity. Increasing temperature increases randomness, worsening parameter accuracy. Removing the tool doesn't solve the problem. Adding alternatives increases complexity without fixing the root cause.

ul.li: Enum constraints in the parameter schema are especially effective — they limit the LLM to valid values rather than relying on it to generate valid strings from a description.
Tool descriptions should include negative examples ("do NOT use this for...") to help the LLM avoid common misuse patterns.
Databricks Agent Framework validates tool calls against their JSON schemas before execution, providing clear error messages the agent can use to self-correct.

question.title: Multi-Agent System Design

question.question-text: Which architectural pattern best handles this multi-stage workflow?

Three independent chatbots with no communication between them
Removing the AI and using manual processes
A multi-agent system with specialized agents for each stage, coordinated by an orchestrator agent that routes tasks and manages handoffs
