hint.content: Consider the pattern where each stage is handled by a specialist agent and a coordinator manages the flow between them.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A multi-agent system assigns each stage to a specialized agent with its own tools, system prompt, and model configuration optimized for that task. An orchestrator agent coordinates the workflow: it routes the initial request to the requirements-gathering agent, passes the output to the design agent, and finally to the implementation agent. This division of labor improves quality because each agent has a focused scope. A single agent with everything in one prompt suffers from attention dilution. Independent chatbots can't pass context between stages.

ul.li: Mosaic AI Agent Framework supports composing agents where one agent's output becomes another's input through a defined handoff protocol.
Each sub-agent can use a different model optimized for its task — a smaller, faster model for requirements extraction and a more capable model for code generation.
Evaluating multi-agent systems requires both end-to-end metrics (does the final output meet requirements?) and per-agent metrics (did each agent perform its stage correctly?).

question.title: Retrieval Tool for Agents
question.scenario: An AI agent answers HR policy questions. It has access to a vector search tool connected to the company's policy document index. The agent sometimes calls the tool with overly broad queries, retrieves irrelevant documents, and generates inaccurate answers. Other times it skips retrieval entirely and hallucinates policies that don't exist.
question.question-text: What is the best approach to improve the agent's retrieval tool usage?

choices.choice: Add explicit instructions in the system prompt that the agent must always consult the retrieval tool for policy questions and should formulate specific search queries based on the user's question
Force the agent to always retrieve exactly 50 documents for every question
Remove the retrieval tool and rely on the LLM's training knowledge for HR policies
Replace the vector search with a keyword search engine

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about how system prompt instructions can guide the agent's decision to use the retrieval tool and improve the quality of its search queries.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Explicit system prompt instructions should tell the agent when it must use the retrieval tool (always for policy questions — never rely on training knowledge) and how to formulate effective queries (extract the specific policy topic from the user's question rather than passing the raw question). This addresses both problems: skipping retrieval and using overly broad queries. Removing retrieval guarantees hallucination. Forcing 50 documents always wastes context. Keyword search doesn't fix the query formulation problem.

ul.li: Mandatory tool use can be enforced at the framework level — Mosaic AI Agent Framework supports "required" tool annotations that prevent the agent from generating a response without first consulting specified tools.
Query decomposition instructions (e.g., "break complex questions into individual policy topics and retrieve for each") improve recall for multi-part questions.
Logging retrieval queries alongside user questions enables analysis of query drift — cases where the agent's reformulated query diverges semantically from the user's intent.

question.title: Delta Tables for Knowledge Bases
question.scenario: A team is building a knowledge base for their RAG application. They need to store processed documents with their text content, metadata, and embedding vectors. The data must support ACID transactions, time travel for debugging, and efficient updates when documents are modified.
question.question-text: Which Databricks storage format is best suited for storing the RAG knowledge base?

choices.choice: Plain text files stored in cloud object storage
Delta tables, which provide ACID transactions, time travel, and efficient upserts for document management
JSON files in a mounted filesystem
A relational database outside of Databricks

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which storage format is native to Databricks and provides transactional guarantees, versioning, and schema enforcement.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Delta tables are the native storage format on Databricks, providing ACID transactions (safe concurrent reads and writes), time travel (query previous versions for debugging or rollback), schema enforcement (prevent corrupt data from entering the knowledge base), and efficient MERGE operations for upserting modified documents. They integrate seamlessly with Vector Search through Delta Sync Indexes. Plain text and JSON files lack transactions and schema enforcement. An external relational database adds unnecessary complexity and doesn't integrate with Databricks ecosystem features.

ul.li: Delta tables with Change Data Feed (CDF) enabled allow Vector Search Delta Sync Indexes to incrementally process only changed rows, avoiding full reindexing.
Liquid clustering in Delta tables optimizes data layout for common query patterns (e.g., filtering by document category or date), improving retrieval performance.
Time travel enables A/B comparisons of RAG quality before and after knowledge base updates by querying the vector index at different versions.

question.title: Document Ingestion Pipeline
question.scenario: A company has thousands of PDF, Word, and HTML documents that need to be ingested into a RAG knowledge base. The pipeline must extract text, split into chunks, generate embeddings, and store the results in a Delta table with a synchronized vector index. New documents arrive daily.
question.question-text: Which Databricks-native approach builds a reliable, incremental document ingestion pipeline?

choices.choice: A manual notebook that re-processes all documents daily
Exporting all documents to a third-party ETL tool outside Databricks
A medallion architecture pipeline using Auto Loader for incremental file ingestion, Delta tables for each processing stage, and Delta Sync for automatic vector index updates
A cron job that copies files directly into the vector index without processing

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the approach that uses Databricks-native tools for incremental ingestion, structured processing stages, and automatic vector synchronization.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A medallion architecture pipeline processes documents through stages: Auto Loader incrementally detects and ingests new files from cloud storage (bronze), text extraction and chunking transform raw documents into structured chunks (silver), embedding generation enriches chunks with vectors (gold), and Delta Sync automatically updates the vector search index. Each stage is a Delta table, providing checkpoints, schema enforcement, and recoverability. Manual re-processing is wasteful and error-prone. External ETL adds complexity. Direct file copying skips essential processing.

ul.li: Auto Loader uses cloud-native file notification (AWS SNS/SQS, Azure Event Grid, GCP Pub/Sub) for efficient file discovery without directory listing.
The bronze-to-silver transformation can use Spark UDFs for text extraction (with libraries like pypdf, python-docx, or unstructured) parallelized across the cluster.
Embedding generation at the silver-to-gold stage can call a Model Serving embedding endpoint using ai_query() in Spark SQL or batch inference with mlflow.pyfunc.

question.title: Data Quality for GenAI
question.scenario: A RAG application is producing incorrect answers. Investigation reveals that the knowledge base contains duplicate documents, outdated versions alongside current versions, and chunks with garbled text from failed PDF extraction. The vector index faithfully represents this noisy data.
question.question-text: Which step should be prioritized to improve RAG answer quality?

choices.choice: Switching to a more powerful LLM to compensate for data quality issues
Increasing the number of retrieved chunks to 100
Adding more documents to dilute the impact of bad ones
Implementing data quality checks in the ingestion pipeline: deduplication, version management, and text extraction validation before indexing

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Garbage in, garbage out — the root cause is data quality, not model capability or retrieval quantity.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Data quality is the foundation of RAG performance. Deduplication removes redundant content that wastes retrieval slots. Version management ensures only the current version of each document is indexed. Text extraction validation catches garbled content before it enters the knowledge base. These fixes address the root cause. A more powerful LLM cannot reason correctly about contradictory or garbled source material. More chunks amplify noise. Adding more documents doesn't fix existing problems.

ul.li: Databricks Delta Lake expectations (constraints) can enforce data quality rules at write time — reject or quarantine rows that fail validation (e.g., empty text, below minimum chunk length).
MinHash or SimHash near-duplicate detection can identify semantically similar documents that differ only in formatting or minor edits.
A metadata column tracking document version and source enables filtering the vector index to only current documents, without physically deleting historical versions from the Delta table.

question.title: Embedding Generation at Scale
question.scenario: A team has 5 million document chunks that need to be embedded for a vector search index. Running the embedding model on each chunk sequentially from a single notebook would take days. They need to parallelize the embedding computation.
question.question-text: What is the most efficient way to generate embeddings for millions of chunks on Databricks?

choices.choice: Using Spark's distributed processing with a UDF that calls a Model Serving embedding endpoint, parallelizing across cluster workers
Processing chunks one at a time in a Python for-loop
Exporting all chunks to CSV and processing them on a local laptop
Manually splitting the data and running separate notebooks for each split

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about leveraging Spark's distributed compute to parallelize embedding API calls across many workers simultaneously.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Spark's distributed processing naturally parallelizes work across cluster workers. A Spark UDF (or ai_query() SQL function) can call a Model Serving embedding endpoint from each worker partition, processing thousands of chunks concurrently. This scales linearly with cluster size and can embed millions of chunks in hours rather than days. Sequential processing in a for-loop is single-threaded and extremely slow. Local laptop processing is limited by local compute and network bandwidth. Manual splitting is error-prone and doesn't leverage Spark's fault tolerance.

ul.li: Spark UDFs should batch chunks into groups (e.g., 100 per API call) using pandas_udf to minimize per-request overhead and maximize throughput.
Rate limiting on the embedding endpoint must be accounted for — configure the Spark job's parallelism to match the endpoint's provisioned throughput to avoid throttling.
For very large corpora, pre-compute embeddings and store them as a column in the Delta table, then use a "direct vector access" index type that skips embedding computation at sync time.

question.title: Incremental Data Processing for GenAI
question.scenario: A knowledge base Delta table receives continuous updates: new documents are inserted, existing documents are modified, and obsolete documents are deleted. The vector search index must reflect these changes with minimal latency. Full reindexing after every change is too expensive.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature enables the vector index to incrementally process only the changed rows from the source Delta table?

choices.choice: Scheduled full-table scans using a batch notebook job
Delta Change Data Feed (CDF), which captures row-level insert, update, and delete changes that the Delta Sync Index consumes incrementally
Manual change tracking using a separate audit log table
File-level timestamps to detect modified Parquet files

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the Delta Lake feature that produces a stream of row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) that downstream consumers can process incrementally.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Delta Change Data Feed (CDF) records row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) as they happen in a Delta table. Delta Sync Indexes consume this change feed incrementally, processing only the changed rows rather than re-scanning the entire table. This provides near real-time index updates at a fraction of the cost of full reindexing. Scheduled full scans are expensive and high-latency. Manual audit logs require custom code and are error-prone. File-level timestamps are too coarse for row-level changes.

ul.li: CDF must be enabled on the Delta table (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true) before changes can be tracked — it does not retroactively capture past changes.
Continuous sync mode in Delta Sync Index processes CDF changes in near real-time (sub-second latency), while triggered sync processes changes on demand.
CDF integrates with Structured Streaming, enabling complex incremental transformations (re-chunking, re-embedding) before the final Delta table that feeds the vector index.

question.title: Unity Catalog for GenAI Data Governance
question.scenario: A regulated financial institution uses Databricks for GenAI. Their compliance team requires that all training data, embedding models, vector indexes, and serving endpoints are governed under a single access control framework with full audit trails. Different teams should only access data and models relevant to their department.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature provides unified governance across all GenAI data and model assets?

choices.choice: Workspace-level folder permissions applied to notebooks
Cloud provider IAM policies configured outside Databricks
Unity Catalog, which provides centralized access control, lineage tracking, and auditing across tables, models, vector indexes, and serving endpoints
A custom permissions database maintained by the compliance team

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which single Databricks service governs all asset types — data, models, indexes, and endpoints — under one permission framework.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Unity Catalog provides a single governance layer for all Databricks assets relevant to GenAI: Delta tables (training data, knowledge bases), registered models, vector search indexes, model serving endpoints, and feature tables. Access control uses standard SQL GRANT/REVOKE syntax. Lineage tracking shows how data flows from source tables through models to serving endpoints. Audit logging captures all access events for compliance. Workspace-level permissions are too narrow. Cloud IAM doesn't understand Databricks-specific assets. Custom solutions are expensive to build and maintain.

ul.li: Unity Catalog's three-level namespace (catalog.schema.asset) enables department-level isolation: each department gets its own catalog with independent permissions.
Dynamic views in Unity Catalog can implement row-level security on training data, ensuring different teams see only their authorized data subsets.
Unity Catalog audit logs integrate with cloud-native SIEM solutions for centralized security monitoring across the entire GenAI infrastructure.

question.title: Structured vs Unstructured Data for GenAI
question.scenario: A team is designing a GenAI application that needs to answer questions about both structured data (sales figures in Delta tables) and unstructured data (product manuals in PDF format). They want a unified approach to serve both data types.
question.question-text: What is the recommended approach for handling both structured and unstructured data in a GenAI application?

choices.choice: Convert all structured data into unstructured text documents
Ignore unstructured data and only use structured queries
Use a single vector index for everything regardless of data type
Use SQL tools (text-to-SQL) for structured data queries and vector search (RAG) for unstructured document retrieval, with the agent selecting the appropriate tool based on the question

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Different data types benefit from different retrieval mechanisms — think about matching the tool to the data type.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Structured data (tables with rows and columns) is best queried with SQL, which provides exact, aggregatable results. Unstructured data (documents, manuals) is best served through vector search and RAG. An agent equipped with both a SQL tool and a retrieval tool can determine which data source to query based on the user's question: "What were Q4 sales?" goes to SQL, while "How do I install the product?" goes to RAG. Converting structured data to text loses precision. Ignoring unstructured data misses valuable knowledge. A single vector index cannot efficiently handle structured queries like aggregations.

ul.li: Mosaic AI Agent Framework supports multi-tool agents that can dynamically select between SQL, vector search, API calls, and other tools based on the query.
For ambiguous questions that span both types ("How did the new installation process affect Q4 support tickets?"), the agent can call both tools and synthesize results.
Table metadata and column descriptions in Unity Catalog help the agent's text-to-SQL tool understand the schema without requiring the full table in context.

question.title: Feature Engineering for GenAI
question.scenario: A recommendation agent uses customer purchase history, product descriptions, and real-time session context to generate personalized suggestions. The purchase history and product features are pre-computed nightly, but session context (current page, cart contents) changes in real time. The agent needs all three data sources with consistent freshness guarantees.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature is designed to serve both pre-computed and real-time features to models and agents with point-in-time correctness?

choices.choice: Databricks Feature Serving, which can serve both batch-computed features from Feature Store tables and on-demand features computed at request time
Caching all historical data in the LLM's context window
A manual join across three separate Delta tables at query time
A separate Redis cache managed outside Databricks

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the purpose-built Databricks service that unifies batch features (pre-computed) and on-demand features (computed at request time) in a single serving layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Databricks Feature Serving (part of Mosaic AI) serves features from Unity Catalog Feature Store tables alongside on-demand features computed by user-defined functions at request time. Batch features (purchase history, product attributes) are pre-computed and stored in Feature Store tables. On-demand features (session context transforms) are computed by registered Python functions when a serving request arrives. This unified layer ensures point-in-time consistency and eliminates training-serving skew. Manual joins are fragile. Context window caching wastes tokens. External Redis adds operational overhead.

ul.li: Feature Serving endpoints auto-scale independently of model serving endpoints, allowing feature computation to handle traffic spikes without affecting model latency.
Feature Store tables in Unity Catalog support time-series features with point-in-time lookups, preventing future data leakage during training and evaluation.
On-demand feature functions can call other model serving endpoints, enabling feature cascades where one model's output is another model's input feature.

question.title: LLM Evaluation Metrics
question.scenario: A team has deployed a RAG-based Q&A system and needs to evaluate its quality. They want to measure whether the generated answers are factually grounded in the retrieved documents, whether the answers are relevant to the user's question, and whether the answers contain harmful content.
question.question-text: Which set of evaluation metrics directly addresses all three quality dimensions?

choices.choice: Perplexity, BLEU score, and word count
Faithfulness (grounding in retrieved context), answer relevance (alignment with the question), and toxicity detection
Model parameter count, inference latency, and GPU utilization
User satisfaction surveys collected monthly

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Map each quality dimension to its corresponding metric: factual grounding, question alignment, and harmful content detection.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Faithfulness measures whether claims in the answer are supported by the retrieved documents (factual grounding). Answer relevance measures whether the response actually addresses the user's question (relevance). Toxicity detection identifies harmful, biased, or inappropriate content (safety). These three metrics directly cover the stated quality dimensions. Perplexity and BLEU measure language model quality, not RAG-specific quality. Parameter count and latency are operational metrics, not quality metrics. Monthly surveys are too slow for iterative improvement.

ul.li: MLflow's mlflow.evaluate() function computes these metrics automatically using LLM judges — a separate LLM scores faithfulness, relevance, and toxicity for each response.
Faithfulness evaluation requires both the generated answer and the retrieved context as inputs, while relevance evaluation requires the answer and the original question.
Custom LLM judge metrics can be defined for domain-specific quality dimensions (e.g., regulatory compliance, medical accuracy) beyond the built-in metrics.

question.title: Human Evaluation vs Automated Evaluation
question.scenario: A team is deciding how to evaluate their GenAI application before production launch. They have limited budget for human evaluators but need thorough quality assessment. They want to understand when automated evaluation is sufficient and when human evaluation is necessary.
question.question-text: When is human evaluation most critical for GenAI applications?

choices.choice: Human evaluation is never needed — automated metrics are always sufficient
Human evaluation should replace all automated metrics
Human evaluation is critical for subjective quality dimensions like tone, helpfulness, and nuanced correctness that automated metrics cannot reliably capture
Human evaluation is only needed for spelling and grammar checks

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which quality aspects require human judgment because they involve subjective assessments that metrics cannot fully automate.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Automated metrics (faithfulness, toxicity, relevance scores) are efficient for consistent, scalable evaluation but struggle with subjective dimensions: Is the tone appropriate for the audience? Is the explanation genuinely helpful? Is a technically correct answer misleadingly incomplete? Human evaluation fills these gaps. The best approach combines automated metrics for scalable regression testing with targeted human evaluation for subjective quality and edge cases. Neither approach alone is sufficient, and human evaluation certainly addresses more than spelling.

ul.li: Databricks supports human feedback collection through review applications built with Mosaic AI Agent Evaluation, where reviewers rate agent responses on configurable rubrics.
Inter-annotator agreement metrics (like Cohen's kappa) measure consistency between human evaluators, ensuring evaluation quality.
Human evaluation data can be used to fine-tune LLM judges, creating automated metrics that better approximate human judgment for domain-specific tasks.

question.title: Inference Table Monitoring
question.scenario: A production GenAI application has been running for three months. The team notices that user satisfaction has been declining, but the model and prompts haven't changed. They suspect that the nature of user queries has shifted over time, causing the model to encounter questions outside its training distribution.
question.question-text: Which Databricks feature helps detect this kind of input distribution drift in a production GenAI application?

choices.choice: Manually reviewing a random sample of queries each week
Retraining the model weekly regardless of drift
Increasing the model's context window to handle new topics
Inference tables with Lakehouse Monitoring, which logs all requests and responses and can detect statistical drift in input distributions over time

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the feature that automatically logs all production requests and provides statistical monitoring to detect changes in input patterns.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Inference tables automatically log every request and response from Model Serving endpoints to a Delta table. Lakehouse Monitoring analyzes this data over time, detecting statistical drift in input distributions (new topics, changing query patterns, novel vocabulary). This enables proactive identification of the root cause: queries are shifting away from what the model handles well. Manual review is not scalable. Weekly retraining is wasteful and doesn't target the actual problem. Context window size doesn't address distribution drift.

ul.li: Monitoring profiles can track text statistics (query length, language distribution, topic clusters) and flag anomalies when distributions shift beyond configured thresholds.
Embedding-based drift detection clusters query embeddings over time and alerts when new clusters emerge that don't match the training distribution.
Combining drift detection with automated evaluation (running LLM judges on flagged requests) creates a closed-loop quality monitoring system.

question.title: A/B Testing GenAI Models
question.scenario: A team wants to compare their current production RAG model (Model A) against a new model (Model B) that uses a different prompt template and retrieval configuration. They need statistical confidence that Model B is actually better before fully switching over.
question.question-text: What is the recommended approach for comparing two GenAI model configurations in production?

choices.choice: A/B testing with traffic splitting, where a percentage of production traffic is routed to Model B while the rest continues to Model A, and evaluation metrics are compared with statistical significance testing
Testing Model B in a notebook with 10 sample queries and comparing outputs manually
Deploying Model B to all users immediately and rolling back if complaints increase
Comparing Model A and Model B on a benchmark dataset only, without production traffic

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which approach tests the new model on real production traffic while controlling risk and measuring results statistically.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A/B testing splits production traffic between Model A and Model B (e.g., 90/10 or 50/50), collects evaluation metrics (faithfulness, relevance, latency, user satisfaction) for both, and uses statistical significance tests to determine whether Model B is genuinely better. This tests on real user behavior, not synthetic benchmarks. A 10-query notebook test is statistically meaningless. Full deployment without testing risks quality regression for all users. Benchmark-only testing misses production-specific patterns like query distribution and real-world edge cases.

ul.li: Databricks Model Serving supports traffic splitting natively — you can route configurable percentages of traffic to different model versions behind a single endpoint.
Inference tables capture which model version served each request, enabling post-hoc analysis of A/B test results using Databricks SQL.
Guardrails should be applied to both variants equally to ensure the comparison measures model quality, not safety filtering differences.

question.title: MLflow LLM Evaluation
question.scenario: A team has built a RAG pipeline and needs to run automated evaluation across 500 test cases. For each test case, they have the question, retrieved context, generated answer, and a ground-truth reference answer. They want to compute faithfulness, relevance, and correctness scores automatically.
question.question-text: Which MLflow feature automates LLM evaluation at scale with built-in metrics?

choices.choice: MLflow's manual model comparison UI
mlflow.evaluate() with the "text" model type, which computes LLM-judged metrics like faithfulness, relevance, and correctness across the entire evaluation dataset
Custom Python scripts that call the LLM to evaluate itself
Exporting results to a spreadsheet for manual scoring

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the MLflow function that takes an evaluation dataset and automatically computes GenAI-specific quality metrics.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: mlflow.evaluate() accepts a dataset of questions, contexts, generated answers, and optional reference answers, then automatically computes LLM-judged metrics including faithfulness (is the answer grounded in context?), answer relevance (does it address the question?), and correctness (does it match the reference?). It logs results as an MLflow run with per-example scores and aggregate statistics. The manual comparison UI doesn't run automated evaluations. Custom scripts duplicate built-in functionality without MLflow's logging and comparison capabilities. Spreadsheet scoring doesn't scale.

ul.li: mlflow.evaluate() uses configurable judge models — you can use Foundation Model APIs, external models, or custom-hosted judges to compute scores.
The evaluation result includes a per-example scores table that identifies the worst-performing cases, enabling targeted debugging of the RAG pipeline.
Custom metrics can be added alongside built-in ones by defining a metric function that takes (prediction, context, reference) and returns a score.

question.title: Evaluation of Agent Quality
question.scenario: An AI agent with multiple tools (SQL, vector search, API calls) is deployed for customer support. The team needs to evaluate not just the final answer quality but also whether the agent chose the right tools, called them with correct parameters, and followed an efficient execution path. Some correct final answers were reached through unreliable reasoning paths.
question.question-text: Which evaluation approach captures both final answer quality and intermediate reasoning quality for an agent?

choices.choice: Only evaluating the final text response with BLEU score
Counting the total number of tool calls as a quality proxy
Trace-level evaluation using MLflow Tracing, which captures the full execution graph (tool selections, parameters, intermediate results) and evaluates each step alongside the final answer
Comparing the agent's response to a keyword checklist

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the evaluation approach that inspects the full execution path — not just the destination — to ensure the agent's reasoning is reliable.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: MLflow Tracing captures the complete execution graph of an agent: which tools were selected, what parameters were passed, what intermediate results were returned, and how the agent reasoned at each step. Trace-level evaluation scores each step (was the right tool chosen? were parameters correct? was the intermediate result used appropriately?) alongside the final answer. This catches unreliable reasoning paths that happen to produce correct answers — a critical safety concern for production agents. BLEU scores ignore reasoning. Tool call counts don't measure correctness. Keyword checklists are too coarse.

ul.li: Mosaic AI Agent Evaluation provides built-in trace evaluation that scores tool selection accuracy, parameter correctness, and reasoning coherence using LLM judges.
Expected tool call sequences can be defined in test cases, enabling automated comparison of the agent's actual execution path against the expected path.
Trace evaluation enables regression testing at the reasoning level — ensuring that prompt or model changes don't break the agent's decision-making even if final answers appear unchanged.

question.title: Cost Monitoring for GenAI
question.scenario: A GenAI platform team manages 15 serving endpoints across the organization. Monthly costs have been increasing steadily, but they lack visibility into which endpoints, teams, and use cases are driving the cost growth. They need granular cost attribution and trend analysis.
question.question-text: Which Databricks capability provides granular cost tracking and attribution for Model Serving endpoints?

choices.choice: The cloud provider's general compute billing dashboard
Manual tracking of endpoint uptime in a spreadsheet
Reducing all endpoints to the smallest size to cap costs
System tables and billing APIs that log per-endpoint token usage, compute hours, and cost, queryable via Databricks SQL for attribution analysis

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the Databricks-native data source that records per-endpoint usage metrics in a queryable format for cost attribution.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Databricks system tables and billing APIs log detailed per-endpoint metrics: token counts (input and output), compute hours, and associated costs. These are stored as Delta tables queryable via Databricks SQL, enabling dashboards that break down costs by endpoint, team (using tags), time period, and use case. This provides the granular attribution needed to identify cost drivers. Cloud billing dashboards show total Databricks spend but not per-endpoint breakdowns. Manual tracking is error-prone and not scalable. Reducing endpoint sizes may break SLAs.

ul.li: Endpoint tags (key-value pairs) enable cost attribution by team, project, or environment (dev/staging/prod) when queried against billing system tables.
Token-level cost tracking distinguishes between input tokens (cheaper) and output tokens (more expensive), enabling optimization of prompt length vs. response length.
Cost anomaly alerts can be built using Lakehouse Monitoring on billing system tables, flagging unexpected cost spikes before they accumulate over a billing period.

question.title: Regression Testing for GenAI
question.scenario: A team is updating the system prompt for their production chatbot. They want to ensure the new prompt does not degrade quality on any of the known use cases. They have a curated set of 100 golden question-answer pairs representing critical scenarios.
question.question-text: What is the best practice for validating that a prompt change does not cause quality regression?

choices.choice: Running the golden test set against both the old and new prompts, comparing evaluation metrics, and only deploying if the new prompt matches or exceeds the old prompt's scores
Testing the new prompt with one question and deploying if it looks good
Deploying the new prompt immediately and monitoring for user complaints
Asking a colleague to read the new prompt and approve it based on intuition

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the systematic approach that uses a curated test set to compare old vs. new performance before any production change.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Regression testing with a golden dataset is the standard practice for validating GenAI changes. Running the same 100 question-answer pairs through both the old and new prompt configurations, computing evaluation metrics (faithfulness, relevance, correctness) for each, and comparing the results provides objective evidence of improvement or degradation. Only deploy if the new prompt matches or exceeds the old prompt's aggregate scores. A single test is statistically meaningless. Deploying without testing risks production quality. Intuition-based review misses subtle regressions.

ul.li: MLflow's evaluation comparison view lets you diff two runs side by side, highlighting per-example score changes and identifying specific cases where the new prompt regresses.
Golden test sets should be version-controlled and expanded over time — every production bug should become a new test case to prevent recurrence.
CI/CD pipelines can automate regression testing, blocking deployment if evaluation scores drop below configured thresholds on the golden dataset.

Third-party evaluation tools running outside Databricks
Mosaic AI Agent Evaluation, which provides automated LLM-judged metrics (retrieval precision, response quality, safety) alongside a review application for human evaluator feedback
Production monitoring alone, without pre-deployment evaluation
